design_detail: Narrative review (Biological Psychiatry; read as the Author's Accepted Manuscript) of the epidemiological evidence on cannabis and psychotic outcomes: the longitudinal cohorts of Moore et al. (2007) plus three later ones, summarized in Table 1; reasons the cohorts might over- or underestimate a causal effect (residual confounding, misclassified outcomes from intoxication, reverse causation, misclassified exposure, attrition); candidate high-risk groups (age at first use, COMT and AKT1 genotypes, childhood trauma, cannabis strains); evidence for and against causation; complementary methods; and conditional public-health arithmetic. No search strategy or selection criteria; one informal re-pooling of the 2007 ever-use estimate.
can_establish: How three University of Bristol authors, one of them an author of Moore et al. (2007), weighed the cohort evidence up to 2015, which alternative explanations they considered and how they judged each, and pointers to the primary cohorts and to calculations of lifetime risk, attributable fraction and numbers needed to prevent that assume causality.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes psychosis, or the size of an effect: the review has no systematic search or formal appraisal, its updated pooled estimate is given without methods or inputs, and its risk and prevention figures are conditional calculations, several without stated inputs.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Table 1 gives each cohort's sample size and, in brackets, the number with the outcome: ECA 2295 (477), NEMESIS 4045 (38), Swedish conscripts 50087 (362), Dunedin 759 (25), Christchurch 1265 (not given), EDSP 2437 (424), NPMS 1795 (134), Zurich 591 with 2200 records (221), California 41670 (174), ALSPAC 1756 (97) (AM pp. 19-21).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria beyond scope: longitudinal cohort studies of cannabis and psychotic outcomes, with case-control and cross-sectional studies mentioned in one paragraph. Excluded, with reasons: randomized trials of cannabinoids or of interventions to reduce use (follow-up too short), case studies, and studies relying on a diagnosis of cannabis-induced psychotic disorder, which the authors say presupposes a causal role and has no robust distinguishing features (AM p. 3).
sample.demographics: Not reported beyond Table 1; the Swedish cohort is described as men only (Table 1 limitations, AM p. 19).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The review notes that CHDS, NEMESIS and ALSPAC modelled attrition and found no effect on the findings, under assumptions (AM p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the authors. The cohort list starts from Moore et al. (2007), which Zammit co-wrote, and adds three cohorts without saying how they were found. Several central sources are the authors' own: Moore et al. (2007), the Swedish conscript follow-up and the NPMS report (Zammit), ALSPAC (Gage, Hickman, Zammit), the numbers-needed-to-prevent paper (Hickman, Zammit), and papers by Gage or Zammit on potency, Mendelian randomization, specificity and gene-environment interaction.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited cohorts (Table 1): daily use (ECA); ever use and frequency (NEMESIS); cumulative use by conscription (Swedish conscripts); ever use by age 15 or 18 (Dunedin); use and dependence (Christchurch); use at least 5 times (EDSP); dependence on a 3-level measure (NPMS); heaviness of use on a 3-level measure (Zurich); hospitalisation with a diagnosis of cannabis abuse, as Table 1 labels it, or cannabis use disorder in the text (California); cumulative use on 4 levels (ALSPAC). All self-report except the California hospital diagnosis.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors argue that self-report misclassifies use, that the THC:CBD ratio of what people used is unknown in these cohorts, and that hair biomarkers index only recent heavy use (AM p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed for ALSPAC, where adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use attenuated the association to the null, with the authors noting the difficulty of separating confounding from mediation and the risk of over-adjustment (AM p. 5); and as specificity of exposure, found in some studies but not all (AM p. 10). Otherwise as adjusted in the primary studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; intoxication as a source of misclassified psychosis outcomes is discussed (AM p. 6).

comparison.controls: People in each cohort who did not use cannabis (people who had never used it, for the 2007 pooled estimates); in the California study, people hospitalised for appendicitis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name early-life attachment, abuse and trauma as rarely adjusted for, and shared genetic effects as not adequately adjusted for; prodromal symptoms missed at baseline screening are considered and judged unlikely to explain the association (AM pp. 6-7).

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited cohorts: psychotic experiences or symptoms by interview or self-report (ECA, NEMESIS, Christchurch, EDSP, NPMS, Zurich, ALSPAC), schizophreniform disorder (Dunedin), and hospital diagnosis of schizophrenia (Swedish conscripts, California) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Table 1 lists strengths and limitations of each cohort; no formal appraisal tool.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive psychotic symptoms and disorders only; the authors set aside cognitive features of schizophrenia (AM p. 11).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis apart from one informal re-pooling).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, with the primary source each comes from. Swedish conscripts (Zammit et al. 2002): about 3-fold risk of schizophrenia by 45 for use more than 50 times by 18 (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5); Table 1 gives a linear trend of 1.2 (1.1 to 1.4). Dunedin (Arseneault et al. 2002): schizophreniform disorder at 26 after use by 15, OR 11.4 (1.8 to 70.5); first use 15 to 18, 2.0 (0.8 to 5.0); Table 1 gives 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04) for ever use by 15/18. NEMESIS (van Os et al. 2002): 1.89 (1.25 to 2.85) in the text, 2.76 (1.18 to 6.47) in Table 1. California (Callaghan et al. 2012): HR 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12) against an appendicitis cohort. Table 1 also: ECA 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12); Christchurch 1.8 (1.2 to 2.6); EDSP 1.2 (1.1 to 1.3); NPMS 1.5 (0.6 to 3.9); Zurich unadjusted 1.77 (0.96 to 3.24), adjusted not reported; ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76 to 1.65). From Moore et al. (2007): 1.4 (1.20 to 1.65) ever use, 2.1 (1.5 to 2.8) heavier use, 2.6 (1.1 to 6.1) psychotic disorder. The authors' update adding Zurich and ALSPAC, California omitted: 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), p<0.001, I2 19%, no methods given. Attenuation of 60% to 80% of the unadjusted estimate in the three most comprehensively adjusted studies (figures that match Moore et al. 2007, Table 1). Conditional on causality: lifetime schizophrenia risk about 2% with regular use, about 20% with regular use and a first-degree relative (if regular use doubles risk and risks multiply), population attributable fraction 10% to 25%, about 5000 men with heavy use and 10,000 to 15,000 women to stop use to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (Hickman et al. 2009), and treatment efficacy about 20%, so these numbers would need multiplying by five.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The section on reverse causation cites a single cohort (Christchurch) for a weaker reverse association, while a 2005 Dutch study whose title reports prediction in both directions (ref. 7) appears only among case-control and cross-sectional studies supporting an association. Evidence against causation from incidence trends gets one paragraph. The authors do report their own ALSPAC result going to the null after full adjustment, and the co-relative study that points to overestimation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review documents a consistent association across ten cohorts, mostly with psychotic experiences or symptoms; four cohorts had a disorder or hospital-diagnosis outcome (Swedish conscripts, Dunedin, California, and NEMESIS within Moore's pooled disorder estimate). Its own sections report that the most comprehensively adjusted studies lost 60% to 80% of the unadjusted association, that the only co-relative study found the association shrinking with genetic relatedness, and that the two newest general-population cohorts (Zurich, ALSPAC) were null after adjustment; the authors' re-pooled ever-use estimate barely changed (1.46).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the epidemiological evidence is strong enough to warrant a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (AM p. 2), and the conclusion that there is a "strong body of epidemiological evidence" that regular or heavy use increases the risk of psychotic disorders that persist beyond intoxication (AM p. 13). Gaps: (1) the review states that the usual causal criteria, specificity included, are all met (AM p. 11), one page after saying specificity of exposure and of outcome is found in some studies but not in others (AM p. 10); (2) the disorder evidence comes from few cohorts; (3) reverse causation through undetected prodromal symptoms is judged unlikely with one restricted analysis and one cohort's reverse-direction analysis as support; (4) the public-health message is called appropriate beyond doubt (AM p. 13). Otherwise the review is explicit about uncertainty, sets out reasons for both over- and underestimation, and frames its risk and attributable-fraction figures as conditional on causality.

timeline.event: Swedish conscript follow-up (Zammit et al.), Dunedin (Arseneault et al.) and NEMESIS (van Os et al.): the cohorts with disorder outcomes that the review describes first.

Christchurch analyses (Fergusson et al.): fixed-effects regression for stable unmeasured confounders changed little, and the reverse association (psychotic experiences predicting cannabis use) was weaker; Caspi et al. report COMT moderation in Dunedin, which the review says none of eight later studies replicated.
Moore et al. systematic review (Zammit co-author): the review's pooled estimates and the attenuation figures it cites.
Hickman et al.: numbers of people with heavy use who would need to stop to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (about 5000 men; 10,000 to 15,000 women), cited for the implications.
McGrath et al.: association of duration of cannabis use with psychotic symptoms within sibling pairs, cited against a purely genetic or shared-environment explanation.

Kuepper et al. (BMJ, 10-year follow-up): weak evidence of more psychotic experiences in people who had stopped using cannabis than in people who had never used it, which the review attributes to NEMESIS (see reporting issues); van Winkel et al. report a cannabis by AKT1 interaction, replicated once (Di Forti et al. 2012), judged not robust.
Zurich cohort (Rossler et al., 30 years; weak association lost after adjustment) and the California hospital cohort (Callaghan et al.; HR 8.16): two of the three cohorts added since 2007.

ALSPAC (Gage et al.; the third added cohort): association with psychotic experiences at 18 lost after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drugs. Power et al.: genetic risk for schizophrenia associated with cannabis use, explaining a small share of its variance.

Giordano et al.: Swedish co-relative design, association smaller with closer genetic relatedness (cousins to monozygotic twins), read by the review as overestimation from genetic and shared-environment effects. Di Forti et al.: high-potency (skunk) but not resin (hash) cannabis associated with first-episode psychosis in south London; Gage et al. (in press) on whether that reflects selection to extremes of use.

Ksir and Hart, critical overview of the same evidence period reaching the opposite reading (shared vulnerability); they cite a 2013 commentary by the same three authors (Gage, Zammit and Hickman, F1000 Medicine Reports) for a UK rise in cannabis use without a rise in first admissions for schizophrenia, a commentary this review does not cite.

Gillespie and Kendler, viewpoint: the Mendelian randomization studies this review called for (including Gage et al. 2017) found stronger evidence that liability to schizophrenia raises cannabis use than the reverse, and one (Vaucher et al. 2018) an effect of liability to cannabis use on schizophrenia.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited statement of the causal-leaning epidemiological reading, by authors of Moore et al. (2007). The Mendelian randomization studies it proposed have since been done, with results that Gillespie and Kendler (2021) read as mostly reverse causation and partial confounding. Its numbers are second-hand or conditional; claims should cite the primary cohorts, or Moore et al. (2007) for pooled estimates, and use this review for its arguments and its conditional public-health arithmetic, labelled as assuming causality.

funding.funder: As printed: SG is funded an UK Medical Research Council PhD scholarship (grant number SD1708) (Acknowledgements, AM p. 14). No other funding is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no biomedical financial interests or potential conflicts of interest (Financial Disclosures, AM p. 14).
funding.affiliations_note: MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit and School of Social and Community Medicine, University of Bristol. Zammit is an author of Moore et al. (2007), the Swedish conscript follow-up and the NPMS report; Gage, Hickman and Zammit of the ALSPAC report; Hickman and Zammit of the numbers-needed-to-prevent paper. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: As the authors propose: estimates free of residual confounding from large cluster-randomized prevention trials with registry follow-up for psychosis, comparisons across cohorts whose confounding structures differ, and Mendelian randomization with genetic instruments that predict heavy use; and cohorts that measure the THC and CBD content of what people use.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; three cohorts are added to Moore et al. (2007) without saying how they were found.

Table 1 lists strengths and limitations per cohort and the interpretation sections weigh each bias in turn, but there is no formal tool and the genetically informed and gene-environment studies are summarized without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The pooled estimates, the Swedish and NPMS cohorts, ALSPAC, the numbers-needed-to-prevent estimate and the gene-environment commentaries cited for non-replication of COMT are the authors' own; their null ALSPAC result is reported plainly.

The implications figures are labelled as conditional on causality, but inputs are not given (baseline risks behind 2% and 20%; methods of the 1.46 re-pooling; the 10% to 25% range, which is not in the cited source as read). Statements without data: people who use heavily are rarely un-intoxicated because of THC's long half-life; undetected prodrome unlikely; the causal criteria all met.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal effect of cannabis on psychosis
domains.note: Under-represented: the non-causal explanations. Reverse causation and incidence trends get one paragraph each and are argued against; shared genetic liability is dismissed on one polygenic-score study. The co-relative study pointing to overestimation and the null ALSPAC and Zurich results are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of a systematic search. The review is well structured and open about uncertainty, but selective, built largely on its authors' own work, and its few new numbers (the 1.46 re-pooling, the 2% and 20% lifetime risks, the 10% to 25% attributable fraction) come without methods or inputs. It may be cited for its arguments (directions of bias, the case for complementary designs, the conditional public-health arithmetic, labelled as such) and as a pointer to the cohorts in Table 1; every figure must be cited to its primary source.

key_findings.finding: Scope and update: a 2007 systematic review (Moore et al.) identified 7 cohorts; three more have been published since (Zurich, ALSPAC, California), and these 10 are described in the text and Table 1. The 2007 estimates are restated (any psychotic outcome, ever versus never use, 40% increase, 95% CI 20% to 65%; heavier or more regular use OR 2.1, 1.5 to 2.8; psychotic disorder 2.6, 1.1 to 6.1). Adding adjusted results from the Zurich study and ALSPAC, with California omitted for its extreme exposure measure, gives an updated pooled OR for any psychotic outcome of 1.46 (95% CI 1.24 to 1.72), p<0.001, I2 19%.
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies, 1st paragraph (AM p. 4) and last paragraph, before Interpretation of the findings (AM p. 5)
key_findings.note: No model or inputs are given for the update. Table 1 says adjusted Zurich results were not reported, and the Zurich and ALSPAC exposures are heaviness or cumulative use, not ever use (see reporting issues). AM p. is the PDF page, one more than the manuscript's own page number.

key_findings.finding: Cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome: Swedish conscripts, dose-response between cannabis use by 18 and schizophrenia by 45, about 3-fold risk for more than 50 times (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5); Dunedin, use by 15 and schizophreniform disorder at 26, OR 11.4 (1.8 to 70.5), first use between 15 and 18, 2.0 (0.8 to 5.0), intervals wide and overlapping; NEMESIS, cumulative use and incident psychotic outcomes 3 years later, OR 1.89 (1.25 to 2.85); California, hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder and later hospitalisation for schizophrenia against an appendicitis cohort, HR 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12).
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic disorder, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cohorts with psychotic experiences: Christchurch, cannabis dependence associated after adjustment for numerous confounders; EDSP, any use at baseline associated with psychotic symptoms 42 months later; ECA, daily use associated, little evidence for ever use; NPMS, dependence associated with incident symptoms 18 months later before but not after adjustment; Zurich (30-year follow-up), weak evidence for schizophrenia nuclear symptoms before but not after adjustment; ALSPAC, cumulative use at 16 associated with psychotic experiences at 18 after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood confounders, attenuated to the null after further adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use (the authors discuss confounding versus mediation and over-adjustment).
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic experiences, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 4-5) and 2nd paragraph (AM p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Table 1, sample size (with outcome), exposure, outcome and result: ECA 2295 (477), daily use, psychotic experiences, OR 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12); NEMESIS 4045 (38), ever use and frequency, psychosis symptom severity, 2.76 (1.18 to 6.47); Swedish conscripts 50087 (362), cumulative use, schizophrenia diagnosis, linear trend 1.2 (1.1 to 1.4); Dunedin 759 (25), ever use by 15/18, schizophreniform diagnosis, 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04); Christchurch 1265, use or dependence, psychotic experiences, 1.8 (1.2 to 2.6); EDSP 2437 (424), use at least 5 times, psychotic symptoms, 1.2 (1.1 to 1.3); NPMS 1795 (134), dependence (3 levels), self-reported psychotic symptoms, 1.5 (0.6 to 3.9); Zurich 591 [2200 records] (221), heaviness of use (3 levels), self-reported schizophrenia nuclear symptoms, adjusted results not reported, unadjusted 1.77 (0.96 to 3.24); California 41670 (174), hospitalisation for cannabis abuse, hospitalisation for schizophrenia, 8.2 (5.1 to 13.1); ALSPAC 1756 (97), cumulative use (4 levels), psychotic experience severity (4 levels), 1.12 (0.76 to 1.65).
key_findings.note: The column is headed adjusted OR but holds a hazard ratio (California), a per-category linear trend (Swedish) and an unadjusted estimate (Zurich).

key_findings.finding: Residual confounding, the authors argue, would most likely inflate the estimates: studies adjusting for more confounders showed more attenuation, 60% to 80% of the unadjusted estimate in the 3 most comprehensively adjusted studies, and few studies adjusted for early-life attachment, abuse and trauma. Shared genetic effects are judged unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little variance in cannabis use (Power et al., ref. 24); a sibling-pair study (McGrath et al., ref. 25) and fixed-effects regression in Christchurch argue against stable familial confounding; but a co-relative study (Giordano et al., ref. 26) found the association substantially smaller with closer genetic relatedness, from cousins to monozygotic twins, suggesting overestimation in population studies.
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Confounding, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 5-6) and 2nd paragraph (AM p. 6)
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the genetic studies. The 60% to 80% figure is cited to ref. 9 (Miettunen et al., on prodromal symptoms in adolescence); by the editors' cross-check it matches Moore et al. (2007), Table 1: Swedish conscripts 60%, CHDS 65%, NPMS 80%.

key_findings.finding: Bias and reverse causation: outcomes based on hospitalisation for schizophrenia are unlikely to be misclassified intoxication; a cessation analysis found weak evidence of more psychotic experiences in people who had stopped using cannabis than in people who had never used it, with very few who had stopped. Most studies excluded or adjusted for baseline symptoms; undetected prodromal symptoms driving cannabis use are judged unlikely, especially where outcomes were restricted to after a likely prodrome; psychotic experiences predicting later cannabis use show much weaker and less consistent evidence than the reverse (Christchurch).
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › ii) Bias, 1st paragraph (AM p. 6); iii) Reverse causation, 1st paragraph (AM p. 7)
key_findings.note: The cessation analysis is cited to ref. 15 and described as NEMESIS (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Reasons for underestimation: random misclassification of self-reported use would bias towards the null, and differential misclassification could act either way; the THC:CBD ratio of what was used is unknown and CBD may have antipsychotic effects; drop-out of people who use drugs or develop mental-health problems would bias towards the null, though attrition modelling in Christchurch, NEMESIS and ALSPAC found no impact.
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Misclassification bias (AM p. 7); ii) Attrition (AM p. 8)

key_findings.finding: High-risk groups: in Dunedin, use by 15 had a higher point estimate than later first use, but intervals overlapped substantially, were not formally compared, and the difference could reflect cumulative use; in the Swedish conscripts, allowing for cumulative use, risk did not differ by age at first use; the authors find no strong evidence that cannabis is more harmful to younger people, though it remains a concern. The COMT interaction in Dunedin appeared only in people who first used before 18 and was not replicated in any of eight later studies; an AKT1 interaction, replicated once, is not robust. Three studies found that childhood trauma and cannabis use together raised absolute risk more than the sum of the two, which the authors call the norm for multifactorial diseases.
key_findings.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Age of use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 8), 3rd paragraph (AM pp. 8-9); Genetic susceptibility and Childhood trauma (AM p. 9)
key_findings.note: The Swedish age-at-first-use result is cited to Moore et al. (ref. 10), which in turn cites a PhD thesis by Zammit; the eight non-replications are not individually cited.

key_findings.finding: Potency: several studies suggest strains with higher THC:CBD ratios carry greater risk; a south London case-control study (Di Forti et al., ref. 48) found skunk but not hash associated with a psychotic episode. Because studies from before skunk was widespread also found an association, the authors judge it too early to assume only high-potency cannabis carries risk, and say future studies must address selection of people to the extremes of use. Ecological evidence that psychosis risk rose in cohorts exposed to higher THC has not been examined. Evidence on synthetic cannabinoids comes from case reports.
key_findings.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Strains of cannabis, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 9-10), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (AM p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Evidence for causation, as the authors list it: consistent association after adjustment, dose-response where examined, transient psychotic experiences during experimental intoxication, consistent neurobiology; specificity of exposure in some studies but not all (refs 16, 23 against); specificity of outcome in some but not all. Evidence against: incidence of psychotic outcomes rose in some studies and was unchanged or fell in others, which the authors call very weak, ecological evidence. They state that the usual causal criteria are all met, while noting examples of criteria-meeting associations later shown by trials to be confounded.
key_findings.locator: Evidence in support of causation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 10); Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship (AM p. 11); Addressing the uncertainty, 1st paragraph (AM p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Methods proposed: large cluster-randomized trials of substance-use interventions with long-term psychosis outcomes (linked registers), cross-cohort comparisons in populations with different confounding structures (the UK and Brazil breastfeeding example), and Mendelian randomization, then limited because genetic variants robustly predicting cannabis use had not been identified.
key_findings.locator: Addressing the uncertainty, 2nd paragraph (AM pp. 11-12), 3rd and 4th paragraphs (AM p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Conditional implications: if the association is causal and of the size estimated, lifetime risk of schizophrenia with regular use would be about 2%, so about 98% of people who use regularly would not develop it; if regular use doubled risk and risks multiplied, lifetime risk with regular use and a first-degree relative with schizophrenia could be around 20%.
key_findings.note: No baseline risks are given or cited; the 20% implies a lifetime risk of about 10% without cannabis in people with a first-degree relative (editors' arithmetic: 20% halved).

key_findings.finding: Attributable fraction and prevention: assuming causality, 10% to 25% of schizophrenia depending on whether risk is confined to heavy use or extends to all use (cited to Moore et al., ref. 10); about 5000 men with heavy use, and 10,000 to 15,000 women, would need to stop to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (Hickman et al., ref. 67); with treatment for cannabis dependence about 20% effective, these figures may need multiplying by five; preventing uptake or progression to heavier use is judged a better target than stopping current use.
key_findings.note: The 10% to 25% range is not in the cited source as read, and the multiplied figures are not printed. Editors' cross-check and arithmetic: Moore et al. (2007, p. 326) print a single attributable fraction of about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) for ever use; multiplying by five gives about 25,000 men and 50,000 to 75,000 women.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that a public-health message that cannabis use is harmful is beyond doubt appropriate, but that harms should be neither understated nor overstated, since overstated warnings may be ignored when experience does not match them. Conclusion: a strong body of evidence supports the view that regular or heavy use increases the risk of psychotic disorders that persist beyond intoxication; psychosis remains rare while cannabis use among young people is common.

reporting_issues.issue: The attenuation of 60% to 80% in the 3 most comprehensively adjusted studies is cited to ref. 9, Miettunen et al. (2008), on prodromal symptoms of psychosis in adolescence; the figures match Table 1 of Moore et al. (2007), ref. 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; claims should cite Moore et al. (2007), Table 1 (p. 322), for the attenuation figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The NEMESIS estimate differs between the text (OR 1.89, 1.25 to 2.85, psychotic outcomes 3 years later) and Table 1 (2.76, 1.18 to 6.47, psychosis symptom severity), and neither matches the NEMESIS estimates in Moore et al.; editors' cross-check: Moore et al. (2007), Figures 1 and 2, give ever use 2.11 (0.78 to 5.71) and weekly use 6.81 (1.79 to 25.91).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least three NEMESIS estimates circulate for different exposure and outcome definitions; any claim must take the figure from the primary paper and name its exposure, outcome and adjustment.

reporting_issues.issue: The updated ever-use pool (1.46) is said to include adjusted results from the Zurich study, but Table 1 states that adjusted Zurich results were not reported and gives only an unadjusted 1.77; the Zurich and ALSPAC exposures in Table 1 are heaviness and cumulative use, not ever use; no model or input estimates are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The updated estimate cannot be reproduced or checked from the review; claims should use Moore et al.'s 1.41 with its stated methods, or label 1.46 as an informal update. Editors' recomputation (AI readers 211 and 242): DerSimonian-Laird pooling of Moore et al.'s seven estimates reproduces 1.41 (1.20 to 1.65), I2 19%; adding Table 1's Zurich (unadjusted 1.77, 0.96 to 3.24) and ALSPAC (1.12, 0.76 to 1.65) gives 1.38 (1.20 to 1.59), I2 13%, not 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), so the update used inputs the review does not print.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 15 (Kuepper et al. 2011, BMJ, a 10-year follow-up cohort study whose authors include Lieb and Wittchen, also authors of the EDSP report, ref. 19) is presented as an extension of NEMESIS and as a study using the NEMESIS cohort, while the review gives NEMESIS outcomes as measured 3 years later.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cohort behind the finding on people who stopped using may be misattributed; check the primary paper before citing it for either cohort.

reporting_issues.issue: The attributable fraction of 10% to 25% is cited to Moore et al. (ref. 10), whose discussion, by the editors' cross-check, gives about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) for ever use and no range by heaviness of use (Moore et al. 2007, p. 326).
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand figure that differs from its cited source; claims should cite Moore et al. (2007), p. 326, for 14%, and not attribute 10% to 25% to it.

reporting_issues.issue: A placeholder is left in the text: the neurobiology sentence ends with a reference to other articles in this issue followed by (refs), with no references given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, accepted-manuscript artefact; the version of record may differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the four references for trends in psychosis incidence do not concern incidence over time by their titles: ref. 58 (Ajdacic-Gross et al. 2009, adolescent versus adult onset of smoking and mood disorders) and ref. 60 (Breslau et al. 2006, race-ethnic differences in psychiatric disorder). Refs 59 and 61 are incidence-trend studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that some studies found rising and others unchanged or falling incidence rests, as cited, on one study each way (Boydell et al. 2003; Frisher et al. 2009).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 1 results column is headed adjusted OR but mixes metrics: a hazard ratio (California), a linear trend per category of use (Swedish conscripts) and an unadjusted OR (Zurich); exposure categories differ between rows.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 values are not comparable with one another or with Moore et al.'s ever-use estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the ECA daily-use estimate as 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12), while the same estimate in Moore et al. (2007), Figure 2, is 2.00 (1.27 to 3.16).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small transcription difference; cite the ECA estimate from Moore et al. (2007) or the primary paper, not from this review's Table 1.

Anchors give AM p. N = PDF page N (METHODS §6.2), one more than the manuscript's own page number. Read: all text, Table 1 (checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi), acknowledgements, financial disclosures and reference list. No supplementary material is mentioned.
